title: Tripo 3D vs Meshy for asset gen
author: Ruskarr
selftext: How are people finding both models? I've got meshy and I'm happy with the results I'm getting for static renders, but I'm curious to see if anyone's using tripo (or anything else) and how they're feeling about the results they're getting?

comments.author: OppositeValue7325
comments.body: I started with Meshy great product and I enjoyed what they're trying to do there. But, when I discovered Tripo it became apparent that it was better suited for what I needed with 3D modeling for game objects, so ended up switching to Tripo.

replies.author: darkshifty
replies.body: Had the same, but are you also hammered into oblivion with their ads like me because of that? 🤣

comments.author: Nilo_Team
comments.body:
been hopping between those too-

if you want game-ready without the blender cleanup loop, nilo.io is free in the browser- generate the asset, hit model settings + LOD slider to knock polys down (~3k ish for studio), auto-rig if it's a bipedal T-pose, then export GLB/FBX straight into Studio

LMK :)

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: Meshy worked better for most things, Tripo nailed a couple hard cases. Rodin was used for all buildings. Meshy and Tripo are TRASH at architecture/buildings. The first pass is fine, but getting that triangle count down has been impossible for both of them.

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: Being a factory game, as low as possible. 500-3k on items (Meshy can't get lower than 3k for many shapes) and 10k for buildings (which Rodin used to do, but the new floor is 20k)

comments.author: shady101852
comments.body: Tripo seems to be higher quality for me

comments.author: meshy_grab
comments.body:
# Key Differences in Workflow

* **Generation Speed & Rigging:** Tripo 3D focuses heavily on speed (generates base models in \~10 seconds) and includes auto-rigging/animation features out of the box. It’s very popular for game developers or animators who need quick character drafts or props to drop straight into Unity/Unreal.
* **Geometry & Mesh Quality:** Meshy tends to hold an edge if you're looking for clean, watertight geometry or plan on 3D printing, as its export engine builds cleaner mesh structures. Tripo has improved its topology significantly with recent engine updates, but Meshy still feels a bit more reliable for crisp static renders and physical assets.
* **Texture & PBR Quality:** Meshy handles high-res texture projection and PBR maps very cleanly for static shots. Tripo is great for fast stylized assets, but its textures can sometimes feel a bit softer on intricate details compared to Meshy.

If you ever run into roadblocks extracting your models or textures from Meshy (especially on the free tier or when browsing community showcase models without spending export credits), there is a handy Chrome extension called **MeshyGrab**.  


It lets you pull raw 3D assets directly from the preview—including textures and formats like GLB, OBJ, FBX, STL, and 3MF—so you can inspect or tweak them locally in Blender or your slicer without hitting credit limits.  


Are you using Meshy mostly for stylized prop renders, or are you working on characters and complex hard-surface objects?

comments.author: Swimming_Beginning24
comments.body: Tripo is better quality, faster, and cheaper than Meshy. Meshy has more marketing budget and influencers. I started with Meshy and switched to Tripo when I realized it was better and cheaper.
